newsitem.title: USA: USDA cuts put hold on world cocoa, coffee reports.
newsitem.headline: USDA cuts put hold on world cocoa, coffee reports.

text.p: The U.S. Department of Agriculture said Tuesday it would not publish a semi-annual world cocoa production report originally expected on Wednesday due to cutbacks in attache reports.

"The Foreign Agricultural Service cut back on attache reports, so we do not have enough information," said Edmond Missiaen, a specialty crops analyst at the USDA. "The attaches are no longer mandated to submit semi-annual reports."
Additionally, Missiaen confirmed the USDA would probably not release a preliminary 1997/98 Brazil coffee estimate until its scheduled world coffee production report in June.
"There are no plans now to come up with an early estimate of Brazil," Missiaen said. "If we do put out an estimate people will be notified."

Although no coffee data was slated for Wednesday, in the past, the USDA has published a widely watched preliminary Brazil crop forecast in the spring. Last year, however, the Foreign Agricultural Office closed its office in Rio de Janeiro because of budget cuts and a reassessment of priorities, Missiaen said.

The semi-annual cocoa data usually updates the October world cocoa production report. In October, the USDA forecast world cocoa bean production for the 1996/97 season at 2.66 million tonnes, down from a revised record output of 2.88 million tonnes the previous season.

USDA said the reduction was based on smaller crop productions in the Ivory Coast, Ghana, Brazil, Malaysia and Cameroon. They pegged the Ivory Coast 1996/97 crop at 1.05 million tonnes compared with 1.20 million tonnes in 1995/96.
The next world cocoa production data, which will include estimates for 1997/98 output, should be published in October 1997, Missiaen said. ((--Patricia Avidan, New York Commodity Desk, 212-859-1640))
